title: wait()/notify() vs Condition.await()/signal() — monitor wait-set vs multiple Conditions

s1_definition.profdef: `wait()`/`notify()` are methods on `Object` — used INSIDE a `synchronized` block. `wait()` releases the monitor lock and puts the thread into the object's SINGLE wait-set. `notify()` wakes ONE thread from that wait-set. `notifyAll()` wakes ALL. Problem: only ONE wait-set per object — if producers and consumers both wait on the same object, `notifyAll()` wakes EVERYONE (wasteful). `Condition` (from `ReentrantLock.newCondition()`) provides MULTIPLE wait-sets on one lock: `notEmpty.await()` for consumers, `notFull.await()` for producers. `notEmpty.signal()` wakes ONLY a consumer — no wasted wake-ups. Also: `await(timeout)` returns false on timeout, `awaitUninterruptibly()` ignores interrupts.
s1_definition.analogy: **wait/notify** = ONE waiting room for everyone. Customers waiting for deposits AND customers waiting for withdrawals sit in the SAME room. When you shout "NEXT!" (notify), you might wake a withdrawal-waiter when only a deposit-waiter is needed. `notifyAll()` = shout at EVERYONE — all 50 people wake up, only 1 needs to act, 49 go back to sleep. Wasteful! **Condition** = TWO separate waiting rooms: "Deposit Waiting Room" (notEmpty) and "Withdrawal Waiting Room" (notFull). Shout in the deposit room → only deposit-waiters wake up. Efficient!
s1_definition.oneliner: wait/notify = ONE wait-set per object (wakes wrong threads). Condition = MULTIPLE wait-sets per lock (targeted wake-ups). Condition = modernized wait/notify with timeout + interruptible.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `wait()`/`notify()` are methods on `Object` — used INSIDE a `synchronized` block. `wait()` releases the monitor lock and puts the thread into the object's SINGLE wait-set. `notify()` wakes ONE thread from that wait-set. `notifyAll()` wakes ALL. Problem: only ONE wait-set per object — if producers and consumers both wait on the same object, `notifyAll()` wakes EVERYONE (wasteful). `Condition` (from `ReentrantLock.newCondition()`) provides MULTIPLE wait-sets on one lock: `notEmpty.await()` for consumers, `notFull.await()` for producers. `notEmpty.signal()` wakes ONLY a consumer — no wasted wake-ups. Also: `await(timeout)` returns false on timeout, `awaitUninterruptibly()` ignores interrupts.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** **wait/notify** = ONE waiting room for everyone. Customers waiting for deposits AND customers waiting for withdrawals sit in the SAME room. When you shout "NEXT!" (notify), you might wake a withdrawal-waiter when only a deposit-waiter is needed. `notifyAll()` = shout at EVERYONE — all 50 people wake up, only 1 needs to act, 49 go back to sleep. Wasteful! **Condition** = TWO separate waiting rooms: "Deposit Waiting Room" (notEmpty) and "Withdrawal Waiting Room" (notFull). Shout in the deposit room → only deposit-waiters wake up. Efficient!

**One line to remember:** wait/notify = ONE wait-set per object (wakes wrong threads). Condition = MULTIPLE wait-sets per lock (targeted wake-ups). Condition = modernized wait/notify with timeout + interruptible.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The trade queue used wait/notify with producers (market feed) and consumers (settlers).** When `notify()` was called after adding a trade, it sometimes woke ANOTHER PRODUCER instead of a consumer — the consumer stayed sleeping while trades piled up. Switching to `notifyAll()` fixed it but woke 50 producers + 50 consumers when only 1 consumer was needed — 99 threads woke up for nothing → CPU spike every notification. Fix: two Conditions — `notEmpty.signal()` wakes exactly ONE consumer. `notFull.signal()` wakes exactly ONE producer. Zero wasted wake-ups.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Consumer calls `notEmpty.await()` → releases ReentrantLock → enters WAITING on the notEmpty Condition.

**Step 2.** Producer acquires lock → adds trade to queue → calls `notEmpty.signal()` → wakes the consumer (and ONLY the consumer — producers waiting on notFull are NOT woken).

**Step 3.** Consumer wakes up → reacquires lock → checks `while (queue.isEmpty())` → queue NOT empty → polls trade → calls `notFull.signal()` → wakes a producer if any are waiting on notFull.

**Step 4.** With wait/notify instead: `lock.notify()` might wake a producer instead of a consumer (single wait-set). The producer checks its condition (queue full?) → still full → goes back to sleep. Wasted wake-up.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ wait/notify: ONE wait-set (wasteful) ═══

  Object.wait-set: [Consumer-1, Producer-3, Consumer-2, Producer-1]
  notify() → wakes Producer-3 → checks: queue full? YES → back to sleep!
  WASTED wake-up! Consumer should have been woken!

  ═══ Condition: MULTIPLE wait-sets (targeted) ═══

  notEmpty condition: [Consumer-1, Consumer-2]  ← consumers wait here
  notFull condition:  [Producer-1, Producer-3]  ← producers wait here

  notEmpty.signal() → wakes Consumer-1 → processes trade (Recommended) 
  notFull.signal() → wakes Producer-1 → adds trade (Recommended) 
  ZERO wasted wake-ups!
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Bounded Trade Queue with Conditions ═══

  ┌──────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Market Feed  │───put──→│  BoundedBuffer (capacity=1000)│
  │ (Producers)  │        │  ReentrantLock                │
  └──────────────┘        │  notEmpty Condition → consumers│
                          │  notFull Condition → producers │
  ┌──────────────┐        │                                │
  │ Settlers     │←─take──│  Queue full → producers await  │
  │ (Consumers)  │        │  Queue empty → consumers await │
  └──────────────┘        └──────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — wait/notify vs Condition ═══

  ┌─ Object (wait/notify) ───────────────────────┐
  │  synchronized(obj) { obj.wait(); }           │
  │  synchronized(obj) { obj.notify(); }         │
  │  ONE wait-set per object                      │
  │  notify() wakes ANY thread — can't target!   │
  │  notifyAll() wakes ALL — wasteful!           │
  │  wait() always interruptible                  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ Condition (await/signal) ───────────────────┐
  │  lock.lock(); try { cond.await(); }          │
  │  lock.lock(); try { cond.signal(); }         │
  │  MULTIPLE conditions per lock:               │
  │    notEmpty = lock.newCondition();            │
  │    notFull = lock.newCondition();             │
  │  signal() wakes ONLY threads on THIS condition│
  │  awaitUninterruptibly() — ignores interrupts │
  │  await(timeout, unit) — clean timeout API    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ BoundedBuffer ──────────────────────────────┐
  │  - queue: Queue<T>                            │
  │  - capacity: int                              │
  │  - lock: ReentrantLock                        │
  │  - notEmpty: Condition                        │
  │  - notFull: Condition                         │
  │  + put(T): void                               │
  │    while(full) notFull.await()                │
  │    queue.add(item) → notEmpty.signal()        │
  │  + take(): T                                  │
  │    while(empty) notEmpty.await()              │
  │    queue.poll() → notFull.signal()            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
`wait()`/`notify()` are the classic thread communication mechanism — `wait()` releases the synchronized lock and enters the object's single wait-set, `notify()` wakes one thread from that set. The problem: ONE wait-set per object — producers and consumers share it, so `notify()` may wake the wrong type of thread. `notifyAll()` fixes this but wakes ALL threads — wasteful CPU usage.

`Condition` (from `ReentrantLock.newCondition()`) provides MULTIPLE wait-sets on one lock. `notEmpty.signal()` wakes only a consumer. `notFull.signal()` wakes only a producer. Zero wasted wake-ups. Additional benefits: `await(timeout, unit)` with clean timeout API, `awaitUninterruptibly()` to ignore interrupts. Rules for both: always use `while` loop (never `if`) due to spurious wake-ups, and always hold the lock when calling wait/await or notify/signal. In banking: bounded trade queue — market feed producers `await(notFull)` when queue is at capacity. Settlement consumers `await(notEmpty)` when queue is empty. Targeted signals: no wasted wake-ups, maximum efficiency.

keyPoints: wait/notify: built into Object, used with synchronized
Condition: used with ReentrantLock, multiple conditions per lock
Condition allows separate wait-sets per condition
